messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Farmer
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir had farmed this land for thirty years, and he knew its rhythms better than his own. At fifty-five, he was a man accustomed to the predictable cycles of planting and harvest, the ache of his body after a long day a familiar and honest measure of his labor. But for the past eight months, a different kind of exhaustion had settled deep into his bones. It all started on a humid evening last summer. He was checking the fence line at the far edge of his property when a man whose truck had stalled on the road called out for a jump. Amir, always willing to help a neighbor, grabbed his cables. As he got closer, he noticed the man’s erratic energy, the way he couldn't stand still, his eyes scanning the empty fields. An unease prickled at Amir. Before he could fully process the feeling, the man lunged, demanding his wallet. The struggle was a chaotic blur of motion and sensation. What he remembers most is the overwhelming, sour smell of the man’s body odor and the violent, hammering pulse in his own ears, so loud it drowned out the crickets.

In the weeks that followed, the memory refused to settle. When his wife, Layla, asked him to explain what happened, he would start the story but then lose the thread, the words dissolving in his mouth. The event existed not as a narrative but as a collection of sensory snapshots: the glint of the setting sun on the truck’s dusty chrome, the smell of sweat, the feeling of gravel digging into his back. Trying to hold onto the memory felt like trying to grasp smoke. At times, it felt so disconnected from him, so unreal, that it was as if he were recalling a scene from a disturbing film he’d once seen, something that had happened to another man entirely, not to him. He was certain that if he could just piece it together in the right order, it would lose its power, but the pieces never fit.

To keep the fragments at bay, Amir threw himself into his work with a ferocity that worried Layla. He was out in the fields before sunrise and wouldn't come in until long after dark, pushing his body to the point of collapse. The physical strain was a welcome distraction; it was the only thing loud enough to quiet his mind. But even that wasn't a perfect shield. Sometimes, while hoisting feed sacks or wrestling with a stubborn piece of machinery, his own heart would begin to pound with the effort. The familiar sensation of exertion would instantly become the sound of terror from that night, and he would have to drop what he was doing, gasping for air, his hands trembling. The farm, once his sanctuary, now held hidden threats.

He began to see danger everywhere. A trip to the co-op for supplies became an ordeal. He would watch other customers, his body tensing whenever someone moved too quickly or seemed to be watching him. To him, every person acting in a way he couldn't immediately understand was a potential assailant. He started sending Layla for things he used to handle. His world shrank to the perimeter of his property. In the quiet hours, when physical labor could no longer distract him, his thoughts would turn corrosive. He would lie awake for hours, replaying the assault not as it was, but as it could have been. He would imagine overpowering the man, turning the violence back on him, the fantasies of revenge so vivid they left him shaking with a mixture of rage and shame. When the anniversary of the attack approached, he spent three straight days from dawn to dusk clearing a fallow field that didn't need clearing, working until he was too numb to feel anything at all.

It was Layla who finally convinced him to seek help. She found him one afternoon leaning against the tractor, pale and drenched in sweat, staring at nothing. He had been stacking hay, felt his heart rate climb, and was suddenly paralyzed by fear. She told him, her voice gentle but firm, that she felt she was losing him, that the man on the road was still stealing parts of him every day. Amir came to the first session looking hollowed out, admitting he was afraid this new, hyper-alert version of himself was permanent. What frightened him most was the thought that he might never again feel safe in his own life, on his own land.
